summary: Richard Watson recaps the long debate on host names and presents what the NIC hoped would be accepted as an official list of formal host names and nicknames. Hosts chose their own names within agreed guidelines. It was replaced by RFC 384.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 289 presents a proposed list of ARPANET host names, nicknames, and network addresses. It records that host sites chose their own names within agreed guidelines.

subtitle: A proposed list of formal host names, nicknames, and network addresses.

tldr.problem: Several host-name sets were in use, and network users needed names recognizable by NCPs and Telnets.
tldr.mechanism: The NIC collected names chosen by host sites under agreed guidelines and published formal names, nicknames, and network addresses.
tldr.outcome: RFC 289 presents a hoped-for official list and was obsoleted by RFC 384.

today: RFC 289 is an early ARPANET host-name list and was obsoleted by RFC 384.

sections.title: How the Proposed List Was Created
sections.content:
The RFC says several sets of host names were in use and that NCPs and Telnets needed a standard set. Earlier proposals had led to counterproposals, and participants were dissatisfied when names normally associated with hosts or projects were not used.

The compromise was to have both formal names and nicknames, with people at each host choosing names within guidelines. The NIC collected the choices and published the resulting list.
sections.plainLanguage: After earlier naming proposals drew objections, participants agreed that each host could choose a formal name and a nickname. The NIC gathered those choices into this list.

sections.title: Formal Names, Nicknames, and Addresses
sections.content:
Each row gives a formal name and network address; some rows also include a nickname. For example, BBN-NCC has nickname NCC and address 5; UCLA-CCN has nickname CCN and address 65; and SRI-ARC has address 2.

The author says people should feel free to change a host name when the situation warrants. The list reflects the names received from almost all sites at the time.
sections.plainLanguage: The table connects each host's formal name with its network address and sometimes a nickname. The author says sites may change their names when needed.

sections.title: Status of the List
sections.content:
The RFC describes the list as one that its authors hoped would be accepted as official. It is a directory of names and addresses, not a protocol for resolving a name to a host.

The unit metadata records RFC 384 as the RFC that later obsoleted this list.
sections.plainLanguage: This document proposed a shared directory; it did not define a name-resolution protocol. A later list replaced it.
